The light at Grey Hook had been burning for 112 years when Tomas came to it in the autumn of 1978. He was forty-two, a widower with a son in university, and he had taken the job because the Ministry promised solitude and a pension. The tower rose sixty feet of whitewashed stone on a spit of black rock where the North Sea chewed the coast into foam. From the lantern room you could see twenty miles on a clear night, and on a bad one you could see nothing at all.

The first winter taught him the rhythm. Up the iron spiral at 4 p.m. to wind the clockwork, oil the lamps, polish the Fresnel lens until it threw a clean beam every seven seconds. Down again for tea. Up at midnight to check. Up at four to relight if the storm had blown the wick. The keeper's cottage was a low stone box tucked against the tower, with a peat stove that smoked and a radio that crackled only when the weather was kind.

He kept a log. Wind, barometer, ships sighted, birds dead on the rocks. He learned the names of the gulls. He learned how the light made the sea look different than it was, how it could make a calm night seem violent and a violent night seem calm. He spoke to no one for weeks at a time, except for the supply boat every third Thursday and the occasional fisherman who needed shelter.

In 1983 the Ministry installed automation. A photocell, a diesel generator, a phone line. They told him he could stay as caretaker. He stayed. The new system was reliable until it wasn't. On the night of 14 November 1987, the wind came in from the northeast at ninety knots. The power failed at 2:17 a.m. The backup diesel coughed and died. Let's produce final.The light at Grey Hook had been burning for 112 years when Tomas came to it in the autumn of 1978. He was forty-two, a widower with a son in university, and he had taken the job because the Ministry promised solitude and a pension. The tower rose sixty feet of whitewashed stone on a spit of black rock where the North Sea chewed the coast into foam. From the lantern room you could see twenty miles on a clear night, and on a bad one you could see nothing at all.

The first winter taught him the rhythm. Up the iron spiral at 4 p.m. to wind the clockwork, oil the lamps, polish the Fresnel lens until it threw a clean beam every seven seconds. Down again for tea. Up at midnight to check. Up at four to relight if the storm had blown the wick. The keeper's cottage was a low stone box tucked against the tower, with a peat stove that smoked and a radio that crackled only when the weather was kind.

He kept a log. Wind, barometer, ships sighted, birds dead on the rocks. He learned the names of the gulls. He learned how the light made the sea look different than it was, how it could make a calm night seem violent and a violent night seem calm. He spoke to no one for weeks at a time, except for the supply boat every third Thursday and the occasional fisherman who needed shelter. On Sundays he wrote letters to his son, Jonas, who was studying engineering in Oslo. He told him about the constellations, about the way the light caught the spray and turned it to silver. He never told him about the night his wife died, or how he had taken the post because the sea was the only thing that didn’t ask him to explain.

In 1983 the Ministry installed automation. A photocell, a diesel generator, a phone line. They told him he could stay as caretaker. He stayed. The new system was reliable until it wasn’t. On the night of 14 November 1987, the wind came in from the northeast at ninety knots. The power failed at 2:17 a.m. The backup diesel coughed and died. Tomas climbed the stairs in his socks because the wooden steps were slick with spray. The lantern room was shaking. The great lens, nine hundred kilograms of glass, swayed on its mercury float.

He lit the old oil lamp from the emergency kit. It was a small, sooty flame. Not enough to warn a ship. He remembered his wife’s voice saying a lighthouse is a promise. He went down, found the old hand crank, and started winding the clockwork by hand, a hundred turns, his shoulders burning. Then he climbed again with a storm lantern, lashed it to the gallery rail, and began to swing it. Every seven seconds, he counted, one Mississippi, two Mississippi.

A trawler, the Marie-Claire, was coming in too close. He could see her running lights through the rain. He kept swinging. The light was weak, human, irregular, but it was there. The trawler altered course. When dawn came, the sea was a field of wreckage. The Marie-Claire made it to harbor with a cracked hull. The Ministry sent a letter of commendation and a technician who fixed the diesel. Tomas kept the log that day in block letters: LIGHT KEPT BY HAND.

He retired in 1999. The tower is automated now, solar panels on the roof, a camera that emails the coast guard. Tourists climb the stairs on summer weekends. They ask about the old keeper. The current caretaker, a young woman named Elin, tells them the story. She shows them the logbook, the page for 14 November 1987, and the oil lamp still on the shelf.

Sometimes on winter nights when the wind is high, she swears she can hear footsteps on the iron stairs, a slow, deliberate climb. She leaves the lantern lit a little longer. Some promises, she thinks, are not meant to be automated.
